extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (agents/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners on applying and documenting rejections under 35 U.S.C. §§102 and 103, including treatment of provisional prior art, priority/benefit claims, common ownership and joint research agreement disqualifications, procedural form-paragraph usage, and options for applicants to overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of priority/benefit claims in determining 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date, consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), U.S. nonprovisional applications under 35 U.S.C. 120 or 121, and international applications under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c) if the subject matter used to make the rejection is appropriately supported in the relied upon earlier-filed application's disclosure (and any intermediate application(s)). A benefit claim to a U.S. patent of an earlier-filed international application, which has an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000, may only result in an effective U.S. filing date as of the date the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 371(c)(1), (2) and (4) were fulfilled. Do NOT consider any priority/benefit claims to U.S. applications which are filed before an international application that has an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000. Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 365(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these rules when establishing the effective date of a reference relied upon for a 102(e) determination; see form paragraphs 7.12 and 7.12.01 and associated Examiner Notes for assistance in determining the 102(e) date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of international application publications with international filing date prior to Nov. 29, 2000
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference is a publication of an international application (including voluntary U.S. publication under 35 U.S.C. 122 of the national stage or a WIPO publication) that has an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000, did not designate the United States or was not published in English by WIPO, do not use form paragraph treating it as 102(e). Such a reference is not a prior art reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(e). The reference may be applied under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (b) as of its publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat these pre-November 29, 2000 international publications as 102(e) prior art; instead cite them by publication date under 102(a)/(b). See form paragraphs 7.08 and 7.09 for related uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph sequencing and bracket insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain form paragraphs (e.g., those addressing 102(e) issues) must be preceded by specific form paragraphs such as 7.12 or 7.12.01. In brackets, examiners must insert specified material (e.g., in bracket 3 insert either --assignee-- or --inventor--; in bracket 2 insert either --clearly anticipated-- or --anticipated-- with explanation; in bracket 3 insert the prior art relied upon). Patent application publications may only be used if the form paragraph was preceded by form paragraph 7.12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow required sequencing and insert specified bracketed material to ensure the Office action communicates the proper legal basis and facts. Failure to sequence form paragraphs correctly can misstate the statutory basis of the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) for public use or on sale
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) based upon a public use or sale of the invention. [2]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form paragraph must be preceded either by form paragraphs 7.07 and 7.09 or by form paragraph 7.103. A full explanation of the evidence establishing a public use or sale must be provided in bracket 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) for abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) because the invention has been abandoned. [2]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph must be preceded either by paragraphs 7.07 and 7.13 or by paragraph 7.103. In bracket 2, insert a full explanation of the evidence establishing abandonment of the invention. See MPEP § 2135 for applicable 35 U.S.C. 102(d) prior art and MPEP § 2134 for evidence guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) applicant not the inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) because the applicant did not invent the claimed subject matter. [2]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph must be preceded either by paragraphs 7.07 and 7.13 or by paragraph 7.103. In bracket 2, insert an explanation of the supporting evidence establishing that applicant was not the inventor. See MPEP § 2137 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents required in a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (A-D)
rubrics_metrics.description: After indicating that the rejection is under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner should set forth in the Office action: (A) the relevant teachings of the prior art relied upon, preferably with reference to the relevant column or page number(s) and line number(s) where appropriate, (B) the difference or differences in the claim over the applied reference(s), (C) the proposed modification of the applied reference(s) necessary to arrive at the claimed subject matter, and (D) an explanation as to why the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on references, include specific citations and explain modifications and reasoning to support the obviousness conclusion. Positively include any reference relied upon in the rejection (even if minor) in the statement of the rejection. See In re Hoch and Ex parte Clapp for precedent. Clear written rationale is essential for applicant reply and later judicial interpretation; issued patents are presumed valid, so the written record must be clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of clear communication of the basis for a rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important for an examiner to properly communicate the basis for a rejection so that the issues can be identified early and the applicant can be given fair opportunity to reply. If an initially rejected application issues as a patent, the rationale behind an earlier rejection may be important in interpreting the scope of the patent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because examiners generally cannot be compelled to testify about their mental processes, ensure the written record clearly explains the rationale for decisions during prosecution. See MPEP §§2141–2144.09 and §2145 for patentability determinations and consideration of rebuttal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to make a provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 using provisional prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional rejections of the obviousness type under 35 U.S.C. 103 based on provisional prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) are rejections applied to copending applications having different effective filing dates wherein each application has a common assignee or a common inventor. The earlier filed application, if patented or published, would constitute prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e). The rejection is provisional since the subject matter and the prior art are pending applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a provisional rejection in the later-filed application unless excluded by 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (including CREATE Act provisions). Provisional rejections alert the applicant that an actual rejection may follow if one application issues. See MPEP §706.02(l)(3) and §706.02(f) for procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome a provisional 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional 103 rejection can be overcome by: (A) Arguing patentability over the earlier filed application; (B) Combining the subject matter of the copending applications into a single application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 of the prior applications and abandoning the copending applications (note the 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph support requirement); (C) Filing an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation (unclaimed invention disclosed in the copending application was derived from the inventor of the other application); (D) Filing an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing a date of invention prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the copending application; or (E) For an application pending on or after December 10, 2004, showing that (1) the prior art and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person, or (2) the subject matter is disqualified under the CREATE Act (joint research agreement disqualification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional remedies: where the earlier application has issued or been published, a terminal disclaimer and a 37 CFR 1.130 affidavit/declaration or a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c) may be used in common ownership situations. Combining applications for 120 benefit requires that the earlier disclosure comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, for each claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional double patenting and terminal disclaimer interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the applications are claiming the same patentable invention, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 may be used to overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 in a common ownership situation if the earlier filed application has been published or matured into a patent. Provisional double patenting rejections may be made; they can be obviated if all requirements of 37 CFR 1.321 are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional double patenting rejections arise in copending situations; filing terminal disclaimers or meeting the requirements of 1.321 can obviate them. Examples in the MPEP illustrate typical fact patterns and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and application of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (AIPA and CREATE Act) — common ownership/joint research agreement disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) provides that subject matter developed by another person, which qualifies as prior art only under one or more of subsections (e), (f), and (g) of section 102, shall not preclude patentability under 103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the claimed invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. For purposes of the subsection, subject matter and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person if (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. The term 'joint research agreement' means a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 103(c) applies only to obviousness determinations under 103 and does not affect rejections under 102 or double patenting rejections. The CREATE Act widened applicability (effective to patents granted on or after Dec. 10, 2004) and the 1999 AIPA change affected applications filed on/after Nov. 29, 1999. In reexamination, applicability depends on grant date. See MPEP §706.02(l) for procedural details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof to establish disqualification under 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent applicant or patentee urging that subject matter is disqualified has the burden of establishing that the prior art is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c). Absent proper evidence of disqualification, the appropriate rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) with applying prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f), or (g) should be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that the reference and the application have the same assignee is not, by itself, sufficient evidence to disqualify prior art under 103(c). There must be a statement that the common ownership was 'at the time the invention was made.' See MPEP §706.02(l)(2) for establishing common ownership and §706.02(l)(3) for examination procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and interpretative guidance for 35 U.S.C. 103(c) terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms are construed broadly: 'subject matter' is construed broadly as in the remainder of 35 U.S.C. 103; 'another' means any inventive entity other than the inventor and includes the inventor and any other persons; 'developed' is read broadly and is not limited by manner of development; 'commonly owned' means wholly owned by the same person(s) or organization(s) at the time the invention was made; 'joint research agreement' is a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement between two or more persons/entities for performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these broad constructions when determining whether subject matter is disqualified under 103(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special rules for applications/patents with legacy filing/grant dates (pre-Nov. 29,1999 and pre-Dec. 10,2004)
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications filed prior to November 29, 1999 and granted as patents prior to December 10, 2004, the subject matter disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) is strictly limited to subject matter that (A) qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or 102(g), and (B) was commonly owned with the claimed invention at the time the invention was made. For reexamination proceedings, applicability of the 1999 or 2004 changes depends on whether the patent being reexamined was granted on or after December 10, 2004.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject matter that qualifies as prior art only under 102(f) or 102(g) was not commonly owned at the time of the invention, it is not disqualified under 103(c). Applicants combining subject matter into a single U.S. filing should still expect 103 rejections if common ownership at time of invention is lacking; applicants have duties under 37 CFR 1.56 to disclose inventorship and dates to enable examiner consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner duties when application claims 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit from earlier-filed application
rubrics_metrics.description: An application claiming the benefit of a prior filed copending national or international application under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the prior filed application. The prior filed application must also disclose the named inventor’s invention claimed in at least one claim of the later filed application in the manner provided by the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112. So long as the applications have at least one inventor in common and the other requirements are met, the Office will permit a claim for 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit without any additional submissions or notifications regarding inventorship differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must examine the earlier filed applications as necessary to determine that the applications have at least one inventor in common and that 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78 requirements are met. The claim for 120 benefit will be permitted without examination of the earlier application for disclosure/support unless it becomes necessary, e.g., because of an intervening reference.
